body:
What does a vaccine do?

A vaccine prepares the immune system to recognise a particular disease-causing organism or one of its components. Vaccination exposes the body to an antigen, or supplies instructions that allow the body to produce an antigen, without requiring the person to develop the target disease.

The immune system responds by activating protective mechanisms, which may include antibodies, specialised immune cells and immune memory. If the organism is encountered later, this previous response can help the body recognise and respond to it more effectively.

Vaccines are primarily preventive products. Their degree and duration of protection vary by vaccine, disease and individual. Vaccination does not guarantee that infection can never occur.

Major vaccine approaches

Different vaccines present the immune system with the relevant antigen in different ways. The basic distinctions are more useful for prelims than detailed manufacturing procedures.

  • Live attenuated vaccine: contains a weakened form of a microorganism that can stimulate immunity under appropriate conditions.
  • Inactivated vaccine: contains a microorganism that has been inactivated and cannot reproduce.
  • Protein-subunit vaccine: contains selected antigenic components rather than the whole microorganism.
  • Viral-vector vaccine: uses a modified carrier virus to deliver genetic instructions for an antigen.
  • DNA vaccine: uses DNA containing instructions for the production of an antigen.
  • mRNA vaccine: uses messenger RNA containing instructions for the production of an antigen.

The last 3 approaches illustrate why understanding the vaccine platform is important. They may all involve genetic information, but the material used to deliver the antigenic instructions is different.

ZyCoV-D: a Gujarat-linked milestone

ZyCoV-D was developed by the Ahmedabad-based company Zydus Cadila, subsequently known as Zydus Lifesciences. It is a plasmid DNA vaccine against COVID-19.

On 20 August 2021, the Drugs Controller General of India (DCGI) granted Emergency Use Authorisation (EUA) for ZyCoV-D. At that time, the Government of India's Department of Biotechnology described it as the world's first DNA-based COVID-19 vaccine authorised for human use, including the indicated population aged 12 years and above.

This is a historical authorisation fact from 2021. It does not establish whether ZyCoV-D was being routinely supplied, administered or marketed on 13 November 2026. Authorisation, manufacturing capacity and actual use are separate matters.

How a plasmid DNA vaccine works

A plasmid is a small DNA molecule that can carry genetic information. In a plasmid DNA vaccine, the DNA carries instructions for making a selected antigen. After suitable delivery into the body, some recipient cells can use those instructions to produce the antigen. The immune system can then recognise the antigen and develop a response.

ZyCoV-D is not an mRNA vaccine. Its delivered genetic material is DNA. It is also not a vaccine containing live SARS-CoV-2 capable of causing COVID-19.

Indian vaccine developers and locations

The following associations refer to the Indian COVID-19 vaccine development and manufacturing information published by the Government of India in 2021.

VaccineDeveloper or manufacturerMajor locationPlatform
ZyCoV-DZydus CadilaAhmedabad, GujaratPlasmid DNA
CovishieldSerum Institute of IndiaPune, MaharashtraViral vector
CovaxinBharat BiotechHyderabad, TelanganaInactivated virus

The distinction is useful in location-based matching questions. A vaccine may be used in Gujarat without having been developed or manufactured there.

Research support is different from regulatory permission

ZyCoV-D development received support through the Department of Biotechnology (DBT) and the Biotechnology Industry Research Assistance Council (BIRAC), including the national Mission COVID Suraksha.

DBT-BIRAC support assisted research and development. The regulatory decision on the vaccine's emergency use was made through India's drug-regulation system, involving the DCGI. A research-support agency and a drug-approval authority do not perform the same function.

From vaccine development to public use

At a basic level, vaccine development involves identifying a suitable antigen or platform, evaluating the vaccine's quality and performance, assessing its safety and effectiveness through the applicable studies, and obtaining the necessary regulatory permissions. Manufacturing then requires consistent production, quality checks, appropriate packaging and conditions for distribution.

A vaccine candidate entering clinical trials is not the same as a vaccine authorised for use. Similarly, a vaccine receiving emergency authorisation is not evidence that every proposed manufacturing facility has started production.

Prelims focus

  • ZyCoV-D is a plasmid DNA vaccine associated with Ahmedabad-based Zydus Cadila.
  • DCGI granted ZyCoV-D emergency use authorisation on 20 August 2021.
  • DBT and BIRAC supported ZyCoV-D development under national biotechnology initiatives, including Mission COVID Suraksha.
  • Covishield is associated with Serum Institute of India, Pune; Covaxin with Bharat Biotech, Hyderabad.
  • DNA vaccines and mRNA vaccines deliver different kinds of genetic material.
  • Trap: A vaccine's location of use is not necessarily its location of development or manufacture.

[NCERT, Science, Class 8, chapter 2, Microorganisms: Friend and Foe, section on Vaccines, pp. 21–22; NCERT, Biology, Class 12, chapter 12, Biotechnology and Its Applications, section 12.2, pp. 235–237; Press Information Bureau, Ministry of Science and Technology, DBT-BIRAC Supported ZyCoV-D Receives Emergency Use Authorization, 20 August 2021; Press Information Bureau, Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, Update on COVID-19 Vaccine Manufacturing Capacity, 14 December 2021; Press Information Bureau, Ministry of Chemicals and Fertilizers, Steps Taken to Enhance Manufacturing of COVID-19 Vaccines, 20 July 2021.]

body:
Why biotechnology is used in agriculture

Agricultural biotechnology can help develop improved planting material, manage particular crop pests and diseases, and make soil nutrients more available to plants. These applications are relevant to Gujarat's cotton-growing and other agricultural regions, although the suitability of a product depends on the crop, soil and farming conditions.

Three important distinctions are genetically modified crops, biofertilisers and biopesticides. Their purposes and biological mechanisms differ.

Bt cotton: insect resistance through genetic engineering

Bt cotton is cotton that has been genetically modified to express insecticidal protein derived from the bacterium Bacillus thuringiensis, commonly abbreviated as Bt.

Specific genes associated with Bt insecticidal proteins are introduced into cotton so that the plant can produce proteins harmful to certain target insect pests, particularly specified bollworms. The proteins do not act equally against all insects. Their effectiveness depends on the particular Bt protein and the susceptibility of the pest.

The first commercial approval of Bt cotton in India was granted in 2002. The official government records consulted for this lesson identify Bt cotton as India's commercially approved genetically modified crop, while other proposed genetically modified crops have required separate regulatory consideration.

Bt cotton does not mean pest-free cotton. Protection against targeted bollworms does not establish resistance to every insect, disease or environmental stress. Other crop-protection measures may still be necessary, and pest populations may develop resistance when the same control pressure is repeatedly applied.

Bt spray and Bt cotton are not the same

The bacterium Bacillus thuringiensis can also be used in microbial biopesticide preparations. In this case, a biological preparation containing the relevant microorganism or its insecticidal components is applied to control susceptible pests.

By contrast, a Bt cotton plant contains introduced genetic material that enables the plant itself to produce the insecticidal protein. The source organism is related, but the method of applying the pest-control principle is different.

Biofertilisers: microorganisms that improve nutrient availability

A biofertiliser is a product containing beneficial living microorganisms that help make nutrients available to plants. The microorganisms may fix atmospheric nitrogen, make soil nutrients more accessible or improve nutrient uptake through association with plant roots.

Biofertilisers do not necessarily supply large quantities of mineral nutrients directly in the manner of a conventional chemical fertiliser. Instead, their living components perform biological functions that assist plant nutrition.

MicroorganismMain roleTypical association
RhizobiumFixes atmospheric nitrogen in a symbiotic relationshipRoot nodules of leguminous plants
AzotobacterFree-living nitrogen fixationSoil
AzospirillumPlant-associated nitrogen fixationRoots of certain grasses and other crops
Mycorrhizal fungiImprove nutrient uptake, especially phosphorusAssociation with plant roots
Anabaena and NostocBiological nitrogen fixationImportant examples associated with paddy cultivation

Rhizobium is especially useful for understanding symbiosis. The bacterium benefits from its relationship with a suitable leguminous plant, while the plant receives nitrogen made biologically available through the association.

Mycorrhizal fungi help plants obtain nutrients such as phosphorus from soil. This is a different mechanism from bacterial nitrogen fixation. Therefore, the statement that all biofertilisers work by fixing atmospheric nitrogen is incorrect.

Biopesticides and biological control

A biopesticide is a pest-management product based on a biological organism or biologically derived substance. Biological control may use microorganisms or natural enemies of pests.

Important textbook examples include Bacillus thuringiensis for susceptible insect larvae and Trichoderma species, which are fungi used in the biological control of certain plant pathogens.

A biofertiliser primarily supports plant nutrition; a biopesticide primarily manages pests or diseases. A microorganism may have several useful properties, but the product's intended use determines its classification.

Plant tissue culture

Plant tissue culture grows plant cells or tissues under suitable controlled conditions to produce plant material. In agriculture and horticulture it can help multiply selected plants while retaining desirable characteristics.

It is particularly useful when large numbers of uniform plants are required. With appropriate disease-elimination and testing procedures, tissue culture can contribute to the production of disease-free planting material. However, the use of tissue culture alone is not a guarantee that every resulting plant is free from infection.

Plants produced through tissue culture are not automatically genetically modified. Tissue culture can multiply existing genetic material without deliberately introducing foreign genes.

Prelims focus

  • Bt stands for Bacillus thuringiensis.
  • Bt cotton received its first commercial approval in India in 2002.
  • Bt cotton targets particular susceptible insect pests, including specified bollworms.
  • Rhizobium is associated with leguminous root nodules and nitrogen fixation.
  • Mycorrhizal fungi improve phosphorus uptake; Trichoderma is associated with biological control of plant pathogens.
  • Trap: Biofertilisers, biopesticides, tissue-cultured plants and genetically modified crops are not interchangeable categories.

[NCERT, Biology, Class 12, chapter 10, Microbes in Human Welfare, sections 10.5–10.6, pp. 211–213; NCERT, Biology, Class 12, chapter 12, Biotechnology and Its Applications, section 12.1, pp. 232–235; Press Information Bureau, Ministry of Agriculture and Farmers Welfare, Study on Cultivation of GM Crops, 15 September 2020; Press Information Bureau, Ministry of Agriculture and Farmers Welfare, Use of Bio-Fertilisers, 7 February 2023; Government of Gujarat, Biotechnology Policy 2022–27, section 5.2, pp. 5–6.]

body:
Industrial biotechnology uses biological activity

Industrial biotechnology applies microorganisms, enzymes and other biological systems to manufacture useful substances or improve industrial processes. Some processes use genetically modified organisms, while many use naturally occurring microorganisms.

The key idea is that living systems carry out chemical transformations. Industry can use these transformations to obtain products such as alcohols, organic acids, enzymes and certain biological materials.

Fermentation and useful industrial products

Fermentation is a process in which microorganisms transform substances through their metabolic activity. A familiar example is yeast converting sugars into ethanol and carbon dioxide under suitable conditions.

Saccharomyces cerevisiae is the yeast associated with bread-making and alcoholic fermentation. In bread dough, the carbon dioxide produced by yeast helps the dough rise. In industrial fermentation, microorganisms may be used to produce useful chemicals or biological products.

Examples of commercially useful microbial products include citric acid, associated with the fungus Aspergillus niger, and acetic acid, associated with acetic-acid-producing bacteria. These substances have applications in food processing and other industries.

Industrial enzymes

An enzyme is a biological catalyst that speeds up a chemical reaction without being consumed in the reaction. Industrial enzymes can be obtained from microorganisms and used in processes where particular substances need to be broken down or transformed.

  • Amylases help break down starch.
  • Proteases help break down proteins.
  • Lipases act on fats and oils.
  • Pectinases help break down pectin and are useful in processes such as fruit-juice clarification.

The important distinction is that enzymes are biological catalysts, whereas microorganisms are living systems that may produce or contain those enzymes.

Wastewater treatment and bioremediation

Microorganisms also help treat organic waste. In the biological stage of sewage treatment, aerobic microorganisms consume much of the biodegradable organic matter present in wastewater.

Biochemical oxygen demand (BOD) indicates the oxygen required by microorganisms to break down biodegradable organic matter in water under specified conditions. Wastewater with a high BOD generally contains a larger biodegradable organic load and has a greater potential to deplete oxygen in receiving water.

During effective biological treatment, microorganisms reduce the biodegradable organic load, and the BOD normally falls. Thus, a decrease in BOD is generally a sign of successful removal of biodegradable organic pollution, rather than an increase in pollution.

Bioremediation is the use of organisms or their biological activities to reduce, remove or transform environmental contaminants. It can be useful in managing certain polluted environments, but the method must be suitable for the specific contaminant and conditions.

Biogas from organic waste

Under oxygen-free conditions, specialised microorganisms can break down organic matter and produce biogas. Biogas contains a substantial amount of methane, which is combustible and can be used as a fuel.

Methanogens are microorganisms involved in methane production. They are important in anaerobic digestion systems and are also found in environments such as the rumen of cattle.

Biogas production and aerobic sewage treatment are different biological processes. Anaerobic digestion occurs without free oxygen and produces methane-rich gas; aerobic treatment uses oxygen to help microorganisms break down organic pollutants.

Genomics and molecular diagnostics

Gujarat's biotechnology research capacity also includes genomics and bioinformatics, particularly through the Gujarat Biotechnology Research Centre.

Genome sequencing determines the genetic sequence of an organism or sample. In public-health research, sequencing a pathogen can help identify genetic variations and support the study of how variants are related. It does not, by itself, prove where an infection originated or whether a particular person will become ill.

Polymerase chain reaction (PCR) is a molecular method used to amplify selected DNA sequences. Depending on the assay, molecular testing can help detect genetic material associated with an organism or condition. Detection of RNA targets commonly requires conversion to DNA before amplification by conventional PCR.

Enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) is based on antigen–antibody interactions. It can be used to detect particular antigens or antibodies, depending on how the test is designed.

MethodWhat it mainly examinesTypical use
Genome sequencingOrder of genetic informationStudy of genetic variation
PCRSpecific nucleic-acid sequencesMolecular detection
ELISAAntigens or antibodiesImmunological testing
BioinformaticsBiological dataComputational interpretation

These methods can complement one another. For example, one technique may detect a known genetic target, while genome sequencing can provide broader information about the organism's genetic sequence. They should not be treated as identical tests.

Prelims focus

  • Saccharomyces cerevisiae is associated with fermentation and bread-making.
  • Aspergillus niger is associated with microbial citric-acid production.
  • Biological sewage treatment generally reduces BOD.
  • Methanogens contribute to methane-rich biogas production under anaerobic conditions.
  • PCR is based on nucleic-acid amplification; ELISA is based on antigen–antibody interactions.
  • Trap: Genome sequencing identifies genetic information; it does not necessarily modify that information.

[NCERT, Biology, Class 12, chapter 10, Microbes in Human Welfare, sections 10.1–10.4, pp. 206–211; NCERT, Biology, Class 12, chapter 12, Biotechnology and Its Applications, section 12.2.3, p. 237; Gujarat Biotechnology Research Centre, Overview, Genomics and Bioinformatics, official website consulted 13 November 2026; Government of Gujarat, Biotechnology Policy 2022–27, section 5.2, pp. 5–6.]
